summary: Defines a cryptographic transform for Secure RTP that applies two related operations, giving both hop-by-hop and end-to-end protection. It lets an intermediary change some RTP parameters in conferencing while the media stays protected end to end.

eli5.summary: Put a message in a locked box, then put that box in another locked box. The courier can open the outer one only, so the inside stays private.

questions: what is an original header block
how does a media distributor change rtp headers
subtitle: Two layers of SRTP encryption, so a relay can adjust a few header fields without ever seeing the media.

tldr.problem: In switched conferencing, a central Media Distributor needs to change some RTP header fields, but the media should stay protected end to end.
tldr.mechanism: The sender applies AES-GCM twice with two related keys: an inner end-to-end layer over the media and an outer hop-by-hop layer that the distributor can open. Changed header fields are recorded in an Original Header Block so the receiver can undo them.
tldr.outcome: The distributor can edit the payload type, sequence number and marker bit without learning the payload. The cost is extra processing and 32 more octets per packet when AES-GCM is used for both layers.

today: RFC 8723 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the double transform and registers its two DTLS-SRTP profiles.

sections.title: Why Double Encryption
sections.content:
Cloud conferencing systems built on switched conferencing have a central Media Distributor (MD). It receives media from endpoints and passes it on to other endpoints, but it does not need to interpret or change the media content.

For these systems it is desirable to have one key that protects the media end to end, while still letting the MD change certain information in the RTP header. A separate key protects the hop between each endpoint and the MD. RFC 3711 SRTP alone cannot do this, so this RFC defines a new transform that applies AES-GCM from RFC 7714 twice.
sections.eli5: A video call has a middle computer that passes the video along. It needs to fix a few labels on each packet, but it should never be able to see the video itself.

sections.title: Inner and Outer Cryptographic Contexts
sections.content:
The cryptographic context has two parts. The inner (end-to-end) part is used by endpoints that originate and consume media. The outer (hop-by-hop) part is used between endpoints and MDs. RTCP is handled only by the outer part.

Key and salt values are generated at the length needed for both algorithms combined. The first half goes to the inner algorithm and the second half to the outer one. The SSRC is the same for both layers because it cannot be changed, while the sequence number and rollover counter are tracked independently for each.

An MD that should change headers but not read payloads holds the outer key only. The RFC does not say how the MD gets that key, and mentions DTLS-based tunnelling only as one possible approach.
sections.eli5: There are two keys. The middle computer gets only the outer one, like a courier who can open the shipping box but not the little safe inside.

sections.title: The Original Header Block
sections.content:
The Original Header Block (OHB) is an octet string that holds the original values of header fields an MD changed. It can record only three fields: the payload type (PT), the sequence number (SEQ) and the marker bit. All other RTP header fields MUST remain unmodified, because the OHB cannot restore them and the receiver could not verify end-to-end integrity.

The OHB is written as an optional one-octet PT, an optional two-octet SEQ and a final one-octet Config. The Config bits P and Q say whether PT and SEQ are present, M says whether the marker bit is present and B carries its value. The four R bits are reserved and MUST be zero. A Config of 0x00 means nothing was changed.
sections.eli5: The OHB is a sticky note saying what the label used to say, so the receiver can put it back before opening the inner box.

sections.title: Encrypting, Relaying and Decrypting
sections.content:
To encrypt, the endpoint builds a synthetic packet with the header cut down to its first 12 + 4 * CC bytes (the X bit cleared, extensions removed) plus the payload, and applies the inner algorithm. It restores the full original header, appends an empty OHB (0x00) and then applies the outer algorithm. Header extensions must use RFC 8285.

To relay, the MD decrypts with the outer key, may change PT, SEQ and the marker bit (and header extensions without an OHB entry), records any newly changed field's original value in the OHB, and re-encrypts with the outer key. If it changes a field back to its original value it SHOULD drop that item from the OHB. The MD MUST use independent keys for each recipient and MUST NOT re-encrypt with the sender's keys, since that would reuse a key and nonce pair.

To decrypt, the endpoint checks the outer layer first and discards the packet on failure. It then removes the inner tag and OHB, rebuilds the original header from the OHB, and applies the inner algorithm, again discarding on failure. Afterwards the application MUST use only the information in the rebuilt packet, apart from the outer PT (for SDP and codec matching) and the outer sequence number (for ordering).
sections.eli5: The sender locks the message twice. The middle computer opens only the outer lock, fixes a label, notes the old label and locks it again. The receiver reverses both.

sections.title: Use With RTCP, Retransmission and Repair
sections.content:
RTCP is encrypted only with the outer key, using the normal RFC 3711 procedures, so it adds no new steps.

Repair mechanisms must work on encrypted packets, since the MD never sees plaintext. When a recovery packet itself must be encrypted, it uses only the outer key, which lets an MD generate recovery packets. For RTX (RFC 4588), cached payloads MUST be the double-encrypted packets and retransmissions use the outer key only. For Flex FEC (RFC 8627), packets are double-encrypted first and FEC is applied afterwards.

RED (RFC 2198) must be end-to-end, because an MD cannot build RED packets without the plaintext. DTMF sent as in RFC 4733 is end-to-end encrypted, so it cannot be used to control the relay.
sections.eli5: If a packet is lost, the middle computer can send a replacement, but the replacement gets only the outer lock because the middle computer has no key to the inner one.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Algorithms
sections.content:
SRTP normally derives keys from a single master key. This transform requires separate inner and outer keys, so it defines a PRF that keeps the two halves apart: the output is the PRF of the first half of the master key followed by the PRF of the second half.

The RFC defines AES-GCM for both layers, with the profile names DOUBLE_AEAD_AES_128_GCM_AEAD_AES_128_GCM and DOUBLE_AEAD_AES_256_GCM_AEAD_AES_256_GCM. Names follow the form DOUBLE_(inner)_(outer). Future documents may define other inner and outer pairs in the same framework.

Each AES-GCM layer adds 16 octets, so the total is 32 octets, and the OHB adds 1 to 4 octets. The RFC calls the extra processing an acceptable trade-off for a secure and simple approach.
sections.eli5: One big key is split in half, one half for each lock. Using two locks takes a bit more time and adds a bit to each packet, which the authors accept.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The transform protects against two classes of attacker: a network attacker who knows neither key, and a malicious MD that knows the outer key. It offers nothing against someone who holds both keys.

Because the transforms are symmetric, they do not protect against attacks inside the group: any member can generate valid SRTP packets for any SSRC in use by the group. A recipient can verify the base header fields and the payload even against a malicious MD, but has no assurance about header extensions.

When an MD decrypts and re-encrypts, the two contexts MUST use different, independent master keys. Reusing the same key and nonce for two plaintexts substantially degrades AES-GCM.
sections.eli5: Anyone inside the call who has the key can pretend to be someone else, and the middle computer can mess with the labels but not the video.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added two protection profiles to the DTLS-SRTP Protection Profiles registry defined in RFC 5764: {0x00, 0x09} for the 128-bit pair and {0x00, 0x0A} for the 256-bit pair.

Both use an AEAD tag length of 256 bits, a salt length of 192 bits, no separate auth function, and a maximum lifetime of at most 2^(31) SRTCP packets and 2^(48) SRTP packets. The cipher key length is 256 bits for the first profile and 512 bits for the second. The first half of the key and salt serves the inner algorithm and the second half the outer one.
sections.eli5: The two new lock types got official numbers on a public list so everyone calls them the same thing.
